chunks: He is One, but not by counting. He is everlasting without any limit. He is existent without any support.

Minds admit of Him without (any activity of the) senses. Things which can be seen stand witness to Him without confronting Him. Imagination cannot encompass Him. He manifests Himself to the imagination with his help for the imagination, and refuses to be imagined by the imagination. He has made imagination the arbiter (in this matter).

He is not big in the sense that volume is vast and so His body is also big. Nor is He great in the sense that His limits should extend to the utmost and so His frame be extensive. But He is big in position and great in authority.
ai.seo_question: How does Nahj al-Balagha describe God's transcendence beyond human imagination and physical limits?
ai.summary: This passage, often cited in Shia theological discourse on *Tawhid* (Oneness), articulates the concept of *Tanzih* (divine transcendence) by distinguishing between God's essence and human perception. It highlights that while intellects grasp His existence, they fail to comprehend His essence, reinforcing the Shia emphasis on God's incomparability to creation. The text serves as a foundational argument against anthropomorphism (*Tashbih*) and physical limitation (*Tajsim*).
